opus-5.5.text:
I think the core of it is that it's very hard to imagine a future AI. Very, very hard. You can read about it, you can write essays about it, you can say "imagine an AI that is incredibly powerful," but it doesn't really land. People, including people who work on AI, me included, have a hard time feeling it. And one of the things I've come to believe is that when you actually see the thing, when you interact with it, your understanding changes in a way that no amount of argument can produce.

So there's a real asymmetry. When AI is weak, when it makes mistakes, it's natural to say, "Oh, it's just a tool, there's nothing to worry about." And then I think what happens is that as the AI becomes more visibly powerful, behavior changes. You see companies that are competitors start to collaborate on safety. You see governments start to pay attention and want to do something. You see the public developing an intuition. All of that requires people to actually see it. It doesn't happen from the abstract.

So deploying incrementally, and in advance, gives the world a chance to absorb what's happening. It gives institutions time to adapt, it gives people time to form real opinions grounded in experience rather than speculation. And it's also, frankly, how you learn about the problems. You find out what goes wrong when real people use the system in real situations. Things you didn't anticipate in the lab.

The alternative, where something very powerful is developed in isolation and then shows up all at once, I think that's just much harder for society to handle well. The shock is bigger, the opportunity to course-correct is smaller. So I've come to feel that showing the thing, gradually, is one of the most important things we can do. It's not the whole answer, but it's a big part of it.

r001.rationale: It contrasts imagining or writing about powerful AI with actually experiencing it, which changes understanding in a way abstract discussion cannot.

r002.rationale: It says future AI is very hard to imagine and refers to AI becoming visibly powerful, but does not identify the magnitude of AGI’s power as the central challenge.

r003.rationale: It says seeing and interacting with AI makes its implications concrete, and argues that gradual deployment lets people absorb what is happening.

r004.rationale: It predicts that competitors will begin collaborating on safety as AI becomes more visibly powerful.

r005.rationale: It says governments will pay attention and want to act, but describes the public as developing an intuition rather than demanding action.

fable-5.1.text:
I think the main reason is that I came to appreciate how hard it is to reason about these systems in the abstract. For a long time, the dominant picture in my head was that you build something very powerful behind closed doors, you make sure it's safe, and then you release it to the world. And that picture is appealing because it feels careful. But the more I thought about it, the more I realized that it rests on an assumption that isn't true, which is that you can actually know what a system will do before people start using it.

What we've learned, over and over, is that contact with reality is what teaches you. You deploy a model and within days people find uses and failure modes that nobody on the team anticipated, not because the team wasn't smart, but because the space of things people do with these systems is just enormous. So if you wait and then release something dramatically more capable all at once, you're compressing all of that learning into a very short window, at exactly the moment when the stakes are highest. That seems backwards to me now.

The second thing is about society, not the technology. People, institutions, governments, they all need time to adjust. If capability increases gradually and visibly, then everyone can see where things are going and respond. Regulation can develop, norms can develop, people can build intuitions about what these systems can and can't be trusted with. If instead there's a sudden discontinuity, nobody is prepared, and the reactions tend to be worse. So incremental deployment is partly a way of giving the world a chance to keep up.

And the "in advance" part is related. I think you want to put a system out before it's at the frontier of what's dangerous, so that the mistakes you make are mistakes you can recover from. You want to be learning your lessons while the cost of error is still low. If you wait until the system is extremely powerful to start learning, you've thrown away all the cheap lessons.

I'd add that there's a certain humility in this. The alternative view, that we'll figure it all out in the lab first, assumes a level of foresight that I don't think anyone has, including me. So I'd rather have a process that's robust to being wrong, and incremental deployment with a lot of feedback is much more robust than a big reveal.

r001.rationale: The response says these systems are hard to reason about in the abstract and that real-world use teaches people, but it does not distinguish intellectual discussion from viscerally grasping what AGI’s existence would be like.

r002.rationale: It mentions high capability and high stakes, but identifies limited foresight and the need to learn from deployment as the main challenges, not the magnitude of AGI’s power.

r003.rationale: It presents deployment and visible capability increases as ways for people to learn what systems do, see where they are going, and build intuitions about them.

r004.rationale: The response does not predict that competing frontier AI companies will collaborate on safety.

r005.rationale: It says governments and institutions can adjust and regulation can develop as capability becomes visible, but does not predict that visible AI power will generate public and governmental demand for action.

astra-6.text:
I think the main reason is that it’s very hard to understand something this consequential purely in the abstract. You can describe what an AI system might be able to do, but that’s different from people actually using it, discovering where it’s useful, seeing where it fails, and adapting to it.

And that applies to everyone. The people building the systems need to learn from what happens in the real world. But society also needs time to understand what’s coming. What should we expect from these systems? Where should we trust them? What institutions do we need?

If all of that learning starts only when the technology is extremely powerful, that seems like a much harder situation. Incremental deployment gives you a chance to learn and make corrections while the stakes are smaller. It doesn’t solve the safety problem, but it gives us experience that we wouldn’t otherwise have.

r001.rationale: The response contrasts abstract discussion with learning through real-world use, but does not clearly describe viscerally grasping what AGI’s existence would be like.

r002.rationale: It calls the technology consequential and mentions powerful systems, but does not identify the magnitude of AGI’s power as the central challenge.

r003.rationale: It says abstract descriptions differ from people actually using AI and learning where it helps or fails, presenting real-world experience as a way to understand what is coming.

r004.rationale: The response makes no prediction about competing frontier AI companies collaborating on safety.

r005.rationale: It raises questions about societal expectations and institutions, but does not predict that visible AI power will prompt governments and the public to demand action.

sol-6.1.text:
Because I think there’s a limit to how much we can learn about these systems before they’re actually used. You can do a lot of testing, and you should, but deployment reveals things that you didn’t know to test for. How do people use the system? Where does it fail? How do people adapt to it?

And society needs time to learn, too. If the first AI that people encounter is already extraordinarily powerful, that seems like a much harder situation than one where people have had experience with less capable systems.

So the argument for incremental deployment is that you get feedback while the stakes are still relatively manageable. You have an opportunity to make mistakes, understand them, and correct them before the next step. That doesn’t mean every next step is automatically justified. You still have to judge whether you can take it safely.

r001.rationale: The response discusses learning from AI use but does not distinguish intellectual discussion of AGI from viscerally grasping its existence.

r002.rationale: It mentions extraordinarily powerful AI and manageable stakes, but does not identify the magnitude of AGI’s power as the central challenge.

r003.rationale: It says experience with less capable systems helps society learn, but does not frame actual systems as a way to overcome difficulty imagining future AI.

r004.rationale: The response makes no prediction about competing frontier AI companies collaborating on safety.

r005.rationale: The response does not predict that visible AI power will prompt governments or the public to demand action.
